Dr Sutton, being naturally inquisitive, decided not to work in general
practice. He was interested to know whether an intravenous anaesthetic
was analgesic (pain relieving) and hypnotic (induces a state of
unconsciousness). He therefore followed the path of medical research.

His thoughts on the measurement of pain led to innovation. He designed a
clinical trial model to evaluate pain relief medication. His model was
deemed a success as it limited the coefficient of variation to just 2%.

Dr Sutton's study involved a laser, because the beam power can be
precisely controlled and will remain at skin level. He also introduced a
switch so that the volunteer had control over the laser. It could be
turned off if the volunteer chose to stop. This reduced anxiety in the
volunteer.

The trial: a randomised, double-blind, placebo controlled cross over
study, was to test whether 1g of liquid paracetamol had a faster onset
of action in pain relief than the equivalent dose in a tablet form.

The arm of the volunteer was painted black. This was to ensure that each
of the volunteers would absorb the same amount of thermal energy, so
standardising the baseline, because skin pigmentation varies. Black also
eliminated the skin reflectance variability.

In the first trial some volunteers had a local anaesthetic applied
(Emla) and others a placebo cream (E45). Those with Emla displayed a
greater threshold for pain. This demonstrated that the use of a laser
was effective.

Refinements to the study were now made:

-   The volunteers would have a button to press which would increase
    power of the laser until the pain threshold was reached and the
    button released by the volunteer.

-   Tests would happen at the same time each day.

-   Participants should not drink alcohol and should be free from any
    substance which could inhibit the results obtained during the trial.

-   No rugby players

Trial participants were a mix of men and women and no difference in pain
threshold was noted between men and women.

Pain is a complex sensation and pain severity brings mood disturbance,
so Dr Sutton devised a questionnaire requiring answers to 17 questions.
These would measure how people felt physically and emotionally, so
identifying the impact of pain.

The answers to the questions would track how a patient felt before and
after using an analgesic during the pain test.

This test successfully demonstrated that the liquid formulation of
paracetamol outperformed standard tablets in early pain management.

Dr Sutton also noted that people suffering from osteoarthritis of the
knee would feel anxious, tired, angry or irritable when experiencing
pain, but the use of an analgesic such as a Voltarol spray would reduce
those feelings, so changing the mood of the sufferer.

Dr Sutton's talk evoked many questions as, his audience being mainly
retired people, meant that, having lived longer, they had probably
experienced pain.

An interesting point made, was that although there had been some concern
that analgesics could cause heart attacks, anger was also a factor to be
considered as it causes a restriction in blood vessels.

The members of Science at Fishbourne were dismayed to hear of the
difficulties encountered in our country when seeking funding for medical
research, and attempted to offer solutions, as they were keen to support
such work, particularly Andrew's research.

Dr Sutton described his other areas of interest and achievement in
medical research which he felt could be of great benefit to health and
to the NHS. He declared his frustration with bureaucracy in Britain,
comparing it with the ease of achieving funding and making progress
elsewhere. Here there is a lack of support, resources, funding and focus
on innovation, making every step in research a struggle and often, a
waste of time.
